item.title: Kyoto Setsubun: Driving Out Demons in Early February — Guide
item.description: Setsubun, held around 3 February, marks the eve of spring in the old lunar calendar and is celebrated across Japan with mame-maki, the throwing of roasted soybeans to drive out bad fortune, shouting ‘oni wa soto, fuku wa uchi’ — demons out, luck in. Kyoto keeps the day with particular richness: its major shrines and temples host their own ceremonies, from costumed oni demons chased away with beans at Yoshida and Rozanji, to bean-throwing led by geiko and maiko at Yasaka Shrine, to fire rituals and huge crowds scrambling for thrown packets of beans and prizes.

item.title: Kasuga Mantoro: The Lantern-Lighting of Kasuga Taisha — Guide
item.description: The Mantoro (literally ‘ten thousand lanterns’) is one of Nara’s most magical events, held at Kasuga Taisha twice a year — at Setsubun in early February and during Obon in mid-August. On these evenings, all of the shrine’s roughly 3,000 lanterns are lit at once: the some 2,000 moss-covered stone lanterns lining the forest approach and the around 1,000 bronze lanterns hanging from the vermilion halls, each flame an offering from worshippers over the centuries.

item.title: Naritasan Setsubun Guide: Bean-Throwing Festival & Access
item.description: Each February 3rd, Narita-san Shinshoji Temple hosts one of Japan’s most famous Setsubun celebrations — the bean-throwing ritual that drives out bad luck and welcomes spring. From a special stage, costumed participants hurl roasted soybeans (and lucky packets) to huge crowds shouting the traditional cry, and Narita-san is renowned for its celebrity guests: famous sumo grand champions, NHK taiga drama actors and other stars take part, drawing big crowds and national TV coverage.

item.title: Chiba Events & Festivals Calendar: From Narita Setsubun to Kujukuri Fireworks
item.description: Chiba’s event calendar spreads remarkably evenly across the year — there are compelling reasons to visit in every season. The prefecture’s Pacific coast produces its most distinctive spectacles in winter (flower fields, whale watching, the Setsubun bean-throwing at Naritasan) and spring (the Isumi Railway rapeseed season, Katsuura’s hina doll festival), while summer brings fireworks over Tokyo Bay and Pacific beach culture. This guide covers the major events worth planning a visit around.
